claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
In the past, having more choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy's TypeScript code bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters instance types not matching the image's architecture, and computes monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS via Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and GeoDeploy won't run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The Pulumi Automation API page exists at /automation/.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.

Jev's choice() picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence; score() rates against a rubric; noul() answers yes/no with a single probability.
GeoDeploy's score() rubrics use 10 levels.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates.
In a single call GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection, five quality scores, two hard checks, and a fallback.
The @typesafe-ai/sdk package exports choice, noul, and score.
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.
TypeSafeClient exposes a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized by default, plus balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.

Weight profile values: latency-optimized cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
Cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), so Jev only decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

Confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 hard reject; new cluster region 0.90 flags top three candidates for human; existing stack region 0.75 keeps existing; ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 uses registry default; node-pool sizing 0.60 uses bin-packing; global floor 0.50 drops AI path.
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts and hard-rejects when residencyOk confidence is below 0.95.
The question definitions are in packages/decide/src/questions.ts.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers) so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.
If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to deterministic cross-provider price comparison while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

`geodeploy monitor` enables self-driving mode, which periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question with options no-change, scale-up, scale-down, or shift, plus a disruption-risk check.
In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy uses a deterministic per-region rule.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals like latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
